newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. agency sees Zaire air drops as last resort.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency sees Zaire air drops as last resort.

text.p: The U.N. food aid agency said on Wednesday a proposed military parachute drop of supplies to Rwandan refugees in Zaire should go ahead only if relief cannot reach them by land.

"We have food already packaged (for air drops)," World Food Programme (WFP) spokeswoman Patricia Clough said. "But we are reluctant to do it -- only if there is absolutely no other way of reaching people."
She said an air drop had to be reinforced with a presence on the ground.
"You need people on the ground to keep crowds back so they are not hit when (the food packages) fall, to make sure it is distributed fairly and so it doesn't fall into the hands of militia.
"It is a very imprecise way of getting food to people," she said from the agency's Rome headquarters, adding that the WFP believed delivering food by land routes would be more effective.
Several countries have tentatively offered to take part in a U.N.-authorised military relief effort but have yet to decide how best to reach hundreds of thousands of Rwandans in eastern Zaire.
Some 500,000 Rwandans have returned home since November 15.
Canada, which will lead the relief effort, has proposed parachuting food over Zaire from a base in neighbouring Uganda, which does not have good road links with eastern Zaire.
Zaire, Uganda and Rwanda would all have to grant permission to send cargo planes in at low altitude to drop the supplies.
"We know the Canadians have suggested (the air drops) and we are waiting to see what comes of it," Clough said.
In recent years food supplies have been parachuted to Moslems in Bosnia and to Kurds in northern Iraq. Some falling crates killed or injured civilians.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, visiting NATO's southern command in Naples, Italy, on Wednesday, said the United States was prepared to take part in the proposed air drops.

Although President Bill Clinton has tentatively approved U.S. participation in a military effort, the United States has so far been reluctant to commit troops on the ground unless the refugee situation gets worse.
